title: Uno, 16 MHz, Timer1 (16-bit, max 65535 steps). Toggle every 500 ms. Smallest prescaler that fits? What does this print?
explain: Steps = 16 MHz / prescaler / 2 (500 ms is half a second). With 64: 125000 steps, too big for 16 bits. With 256: 31250 steps, it fits. Start with the smallest prescaler that fits: it gives the best resolution.

title: Prescaler 256, toggle every 500 ms. Which OCR1A value in CTC mode? What does this print?
explain: The counter runs 0, 1, ..., OCR1A and then resets. That is OCR1A + 1 steps. For 31250 steps you need OCR1A = 31249. Writing 31250 gives a period that is one tick too long (16 us).

title: Your check came out 499.9 ms, not 500. Prescaler 256 on 16 MHz: one tick in us? What does this print?
explain: One tick = prescaler / clock = 256 / 16 MHz = 16 us. Not 15. Then 31250 x 16 us = 500 ms exactly. When a check gives 499.9 and not 500, look for an error above. Do not accept almost.

title: Timer1 toggles pin 9 in hardware, but the LED does not blink on time. Tap the bug.
explain: Arduino init() runs before setup(). It already sets WGM10 in TCCR1A and CS11, CS10 in TCCR1B. |= keeps these bits, so the mode is not CTC and the prescaler is wrong. Write the control registers with = so every other bit is 0.

title: Your code does PORTB ^= (1 << PB5), but the red wire is on pin 9. Which PORTB bit is pin 9, and what does the LED do?
explain: Uno pin 13 is PB5, pin 9 is PB1 (also OC1A, the Timer1 compare output). The code toggles PB5, so only the built-in L LED blinks. Count the labels on the header before you debug the code. The wire was on the wrong pin.

title: analogWrite(9, 64) at 490 Hz (period 2000 us). Divide only equal units. What does this print: duty %, HIGH time in us?
explain: duty = HIGH steps / all steps = 64 / 255 = 25 %. HIGH time = 25 % of 2000 us = 500 us. Steps divide by steps, us by us. Never steps by ms. Write the unit next to every number.

title: 7-segment, 5 V, LED Vf = 2 V. You round 200 Ω up to 220 Ω. Current in mA (integer part)? What does this print?
explain: I = (U - Vf) / R = 3 V / 220 Ω = 13.6 mA. Integer division cuts it to 13. 200 Ω is not a standard value. Round the resistor up: the current gets a bit smaller and the pin stays safe.

title: One 200 Ω resistor on COM, not one per segment. Total about 15 mA. Current per segment, in tenths of mA, for digit 1 (2 segments) and 8 (7 segments)?
explain: Segments are in parallel, so the voltage is the same and the current is shared. The total stays near 15 mA. Digit 1 gets 7.5 mA per segment (bright), digit 8 only 2.1 mA (dim). Use one resistor per segment.

title: Segment A is dark, the other six are fine. Its resistor is 220 kΩ, not 220 Ω. Current in µA (integer)? What does this print?
explain: I = 3 V / 220 kΩ = 13.6 µA, a thousand times less than 13.6 mA. The LED has power but is far too dim to see. Read the colour bands: a dark segment with correct wires often means a wrong resistor value.

title: Period and duty: toggle vs hardware PWM
bullets: Period = HIGH time + LOW time. Frequency = 1 / period.
Toggle in an ISR: HIGH = LOW = interval, so duty is always 50 % and the period is 2 x interval.
Hardware PWM: TOP sets the period, OCR sets where the pin switches, so duty changes and the period stays.
Duty = HIGH steps / all steps. Divide steps by steps, time by time.
A motor or LED sees the average: 5 V x 25 % = 1.25 V, but the pin is always 0 V or 5 V.
